When something is described as "besetting," it means it persistently and repeatedly troubles a particular person — specifically as a fault, weakness, or struggle that they cannot seem to shake off or overcome. It is their characteristic, enduring flaw. Not a one-time mistake, not an occasional slip, but something that keeps gripping them, returning to them, holding power over them no matter how hard they try to resist it.

The single most important idea packed into this word is this: a besetting thing specifically belongs to that person. It is not just a general problem in the world — it is their defining, recurring weakness.

"Besetting" almost exclusively describes something negative. You will rarely — if ever — see it attached to a positive quality. It most naturally appears before words like sin, weakness, fault, temptation, vice, or problem. The most classic and well-known phrase is "besetting sin," which refers to a particular sin or moral failure that a person keeps falling into habitually, as if it has a grip on them.

Some natural examples of how it appears in sentences:

Procrastination was his besetting weakness — no matter how many times he resolved to begin on time, he always delayed.

Pride was her besetting sin; even when she was clearly wrong, she found it almost impossible to apologize.

Impatience was the general's besetting fault — he could never wait for the right moment.

Notice what these examples share: the fault is specific to one person, it keeps returning, and there is a sense that the person has tried — or should try — to overcome it, but it keeps winning.

"Besetting" carries a sense of being surrounded or attacked from all sides by this flaw. A useful mental image: imagine a weakness that follows you like a shadow — to your workplace, to your home, into your private moments. Every time you think you've escaped it, it finds you again. That shadow-like, inescapable quality is what "besetting" captures that simpler words like frequent or recurring do not fully express.

It also suggests that the flaw is deeply rooted in a person's character — not just something they do occasionally, but something that feels almost built into who they are, making it especially hard to fight.
How it differs from similar words

Words like habitual, recurring, and constant come close in meaning but are distinctly weaker. Habitual simply means done by habit — it focuses on regularity without suggesting a personal struggle. Constant just means something happens all the time, with no implication of a battle being fought and lost. Recurring means something comes back, but again, there's no sense of it gripping or overpowering someone.

"Besetting" is more intense than all of these because it implies both the persistence of the flaw and the powerlessness of the person against it. It suggests a personal war in which the same enemy keeps defeating you.

This is a formal, literary word. You are far more likely to encounter it in a novel, a biography, a sermon, a philosophical essay, or a work of literary criticism than in everyday speech. It is a word that thoughtful writers reach for when they want to describe a character's deep, defining personal struggle with precision and gravity. Knowing this word helps you read classic literature and formal writing with greater understanding.

"Besetting" = persistently troubling a specific person as their characteristic, hard-to-overcome flaw. It describes not just any repeated problem, but one that grips a particular person deeply, keeps returning to them, and speaks to something embedded in their nature or habits.
